slides.headline: Shoe wall giving you decision fatigue?
slides.sub: A physio's short list for choosing running shoes without the guesswork.

slides.title: Comfort is a solid first filter
slides.body: Research suggests the shoe that feels comfortable from the first few steps is a sensible pick for most runners. If it pinches, rubs or feels odd in the shop, it won't improve on the road.

slides.title: Match the shoe to your running
slides.body: Think about where and how much you run. Trails, treadmill, long weekend runs or short fast sessions can each suit a slightly different shoe. Buy for the running you actually do.

slides.title: Change shoes gradually
slides.body: Swapping to a very different shoe, like much lower drop or far less cushioning, changes the load on your calves and feet. Mix old and new pairs for a few weeks while you adjust.

slides.title: Watch the mileage, not the calendar
slides.body: Most shoes feel flatter after several hundred kilometres. A rough log in your running app helps. Rotating two pairs can also spread the wear and give you a spare for wet days.

slides.title: When shoes aren't the answer
slides.body: If pain keeps coming back, builds during runs or makes you limp afterwards, new shoes are rarely the whole story. Training load, strength and recovery usually matter more. That's worth an assessment.

topic: Easing back into Pilates after a back flare-up

slides.headline: Back settling? Ease into Pilates again
slides.sub: How to ease back into Pilates after a flare-up without starting from scratch.

slides.title: Wait for the worst to settle
slides.body: You don't need zero pain to start moving again. Most people do well once they can walk, sit and sleep reasonably. Gentle movement often helps a flare-up settle faster than rest.

slides.title: Tell your instructor first
slides.body: Let your Pilates instructor or physio know what happened, when it started and what aggravates it. They can adjust springs, positions and range so the session meets you where you are.

slides.title: Start lower and shorter
slides.body: Try a shorter session with lighter springs and smaller ranges. Leave curls, deep twists or heavy loads for later. The aim is to finish feeling the same or better, not worse.

slides.title: Use the 24-hour check
slides.body: Mild soreness that eases by the next day is usually fine. If your back is clearly worse for longer than that, drop the load a little next time rather than stopping altogether.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Pain spreading down a leg with numbness or weakness, pain that keeps climbing, or changes in bladder or bowel control need medical attention before you get back to the reformer.

slides.body: Our Pilates team reviews how your back is going and adjusts your program so you can build up steadily again.

caption:

Once the worst has settled and you can walk, sit and sleep reasonably, gentle movement often helps. Start with shorter sessions, lighter springs and smaller ranges, and use a simple rule: if your back feels the same or better within 24 hours, you're on track.

topic: Sitting on your wallet and other sciatica myths

slides.title: Myth: it's all your back pocket
slides.body: Sitting on a thick wallet for hours can irritate some people's buttock area. Moving it is an easy change worth trying, but it's rarely the whole story behind leg pain.

slides.title: Myth: sciatica means serious damage
slides.body: Sciatica describes irritated nerve roots sending pain down the leg. It can feel intense, yet most people improve over weeks to a few months with the right mix of movement and time.

slides.title: Myth: rest in bed until it's gone
slides.body: Current guidelines suggest staying as active as you comfortably can. Short walks, changing positions often and gentle movement usually help more than lying still for days.

slides.title: When to get it checked urgently
slides.body: Numbness around the groin or inner thighs, new bladder or bowel changes, or leg weakness that is getting worse need urgent medical care. Head to your GP or emergency department.

topic: Neck and shoulder tension for new parents

slides.sub: Why new parents carry so much tension, and small ways to ease it.

slides.title: Why it creeps up on you

slides.body: Alternate the arm you carry on, the side you feed from if you can, and the chair you use. Small changes spread the load so one side isn't doing all the work.

slides.body: Use pillows to raise baby during feeds so you can sit back with your shoulders relaxed. A footstool can help too. Look down with your eyes, not only your neck.

slides.title: First, get it checked properly
slides.body: A dislocated shoulder needs medical care to confirm it's back in place and check nerves, blood supply and bone. Avoid trying to put it back in yourself or letting a mate try.

slides.body: Your doctor may suggest a sling for a short time. Gentle elbow, wrist and hand movement, plus pain-guided shoulder exercises from your physio, usually start early.

slides.title: Middle stage: rebuild strength
slides.body: As things settle, the focus moves to rotator cuff and shoulder blade strength, then control in different positions. Progress is usually guided by how the shoulder responds, not the calendar.

slides.title: Late stage: back to sport and work
slides.body: Before contact sport, overhead work or the gym, you'll want strength, range and confidence in the positions that matter to you. Your physio can test this rather than guessing.

slides.sub: Common reasons knees grumble on long rides, and what to check first.

slides.title: Start with saddle height
slides.body: A saddle that's too low often loads the front of the knee. Too high can irritate the back or sides as you reach for the pedals. Small changes of a few millimetres can matter.

slides.title: Check cleats and foot position
slides.body: If your cleats point your feet in a way that doesn't suit you, your knees can track awkwardly for thousands of pedal strokes. A professional bike fit can help here.

slides.title: Build distance gradually
slides.body: A sudden jump in weekly kilometres or climbing is a common trigger. Increase one thing at a time, like distance or hills, and give your knees a few weeks to catch up.

slides.title: Strength off the bike helps
slides.body: Squats, step-ups and hip strength work twice a week can help your legs cope with long rides. Cycling alone doesn't always build that capacity, especially for bigger climbs.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Knee swelling, locking, giving way, or pain that stays after rides and disrupts your sleep or walking is worth an assessment rather than more saddle tweaks.

topic: Three mat Pilates exercises to do at home

slides.headline: No reformer? Try these three on the mat
slides.sub: Three simple Pilates exercises you can do at home with just a mat.

slides.title: 1. Bridge
slides.body: Lie on your back, knees bent, feet flat. Breathe out and lift your hips until your body makes a line from shoulders to knees. Lower slowly. Try 8 to 10 reps.

slides.title: 2. Dead bug
slides.body: Lie on your back with knees and arms up. Slowly lower one arm and the opposite leg towards the floor, keeping your lower back relaxed, then return. Alternate sides for 8 to 10 reps.

slides.title: 3. Side-lying clam
slides.body: Lie on your side, knees bent, heels together. Keep your feet touching and lift the top knee without rolling your hips back. Lower slowly. Try 10 to 12 reps each side.

slides.title: How to fit them in
slides.body: Do one to two rounds, three or so times a week. Move slowly and breathe steadily. The goal is smooth control, not speed. Pick a regular spot in your day, like before dinner.

slides.title: Check with us first if
slides.body: You're recovering from an injury or surgery, you're pregnant, or any exercise causes sharp pain or pain that lingers into the next day. We can adjust the moves to suit you.

slides.body: Our Pilates team at Hybrid Physiotherapy can check your technique and adjust these exercises to your body and goals.

topic: Knee pain walking downhill on hikes

slides.sub: Why descents load your knees more, and how to make them kinder.

slides.title: Why downhill feels harder
slides.body: Walking down, your thigh muscles work as brakes while they lengthen. That loads the front of the knee more than climbing. Tired legs late in a hike make it harder still.

slides.title: Shorter steps, softer knees
slides.body: Take smaller steps on descents and keep a slight bend in your knees. Zigzag down steep sections where the track allows, rather than heading straight down.

slides.title: Walking poles can help
slides.body: Poles can share some of the load through your arms on the way down. Lengthen them a little for descents so you're not leaning too far forward.

slides.title: Train the brakes at home
slides.body: Slow step-downs from a low step, split squats and wall sits can help your legs cope with descents. Build up over several weeks before a big hike.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Knee swelling, locking, giving way, or pain that lasts for days after a hike or affects everyday walking and stairs is worth an assessment rather than a guess.

topic: Flare-up now: should you book in or wait it out?

slides.headline: Flare-up today: book in or wait?
slides.sub: A simple way to decide what to do when a familiar pain comes back.

slides.title: Familiar and settling? Try a plan
slides.body: If it feels like past flare-ups and is slowly easing, a few days of gentle movement, heat and your usual exercises is often a reasonable start. Keep an eye on the trend.

slides.title: Not easing after a week or so?
slides.body: If it's not improving, or it keeps stopping you from working, sleeping or exercising, an assessment can help you get a plan rather than just waiting it out.

slides.title: Different from usual? Book in
slides.body: New symptoms, pain in a new spot, or a flare-up after a fall or knock is worth getting assessed so you know what you're dealing with.

slides.title: Needs urgent medical care
slides.body: Numbness around the groin, bladder or bowel changes, spreading weakness, chest pain, fever or feeling very unwell need your GP or emergency department, not a wait-and-see approach.

slides.title: You don't have to wait for bad
slides.body: You don't need to be at your worst to book. Many people find an early check helps them get back to normal activity with more confidence.

slides.headline: Not sure which way to go?
slides.body: Our physios, chiropractors, Pilates team and remedial massage therapists work together at Hybrid Physiotherapy to help you through a flare-up.

slides.headline: Feel wobbly on one leg?
slides.sub: How Pilates trains balance through control, strength and awareness.

slides.title: Balance is a skill you can practise
slides.body: Balance relies on strength, your sense of where your body is, and how quickly you react. Like any skill, it tends to improve with regular, focused practice.

slides.title: Control through your middle
slides.body: Pilates builds strength and control through your trunk, hips and legs together. That steadier base can make it easier to stay upright when you shift your weight.

slides.title: Standing work on the reformer
slides.body: Standing and single-leg exercises on the reformer let you practise balance with support from springs and a hand on the bar. You can progress as you feel more confident.

slides.title: A simple move to try today
slides.body: Stand next to a kitchen bench and hold on lightly. Lift one foot and hold for 20 to 30 seconds. As it gets easier, use one finger, then none. Swap sides.

slides.title: Check with your GP or physio if
slides.body: You've had recent falls, feel dizzy or light-headed, or notice new numbness in your feet. These are worth a proper assessment before building a balance program.

slides.headline: Want to feel steadier on your feet?
slides.body: Our Pilates team at Hybrid Physiotherapy designs balance-focused programs that start where you are and build up gradually.

caption:
Can you stand on one leg for 30 seconds? It's a surprisingly useful check-in.

Balance relies on strength, body awareness and quick reactions, and like any skill it tends to improve with practice. Pilates builds control through your trunk, hips and legs together, and standing work on the reformer lets you practise with support from the springs and bar.

Try this today: hold a kitchen bench lightly and balance on one foot, then gradually reduce your grip. If you've had recent falls, feel dizzy or notice new numbness in your feet, check with your GP or physio first.

Our Pilates team at Hybrid Physiotherapy can build a program that suits you. Book online via the link in bio.

slides.headline: How do you know you're getting better?
slides.sub: The ways our team measures progress, so it's not just a feeling.

slides.title: We start with your goals
slides.body: At your first visit we ask what matters to you. Walking the dog, lifting your kids, running 10km or sitting through a meeting. Those goals guide what we measure.

slides.title: Simple, repeatable tests
slides.body: Your practitioner may measure strength, range of movement, balance or how many reps you can do. Repeating the same tests every few weeks shows real change.

slides.title: Short questionnaires
slides.body: For some problems we use brief questionnaires about how pain affects your daily life. Scores over time can show progress even when pain goes up and down.

slides.title: Your day-to-day matters too
slides.body: We'll ask what you can do now that you couldn't before. Sleep, work, exercise and confidence all count, not just the pain number on a given day.

slides.title: Adjusting the plan together
slides.body: If progress stalls, we review the plan with you. That might mean changing exercises, adjusting the load, adding another service or referring you back to your GP.

slides.headline: Want a clear picture of progress?
slides.body: Our physios, chiropractors, Pilates team and remedial massage therapists set goals with you and check in on them regularly.

caption:
Getting better isn't always a straight line. That's why we measure progress rather than guessing.

It starts with your goals: walking the dog, lifting your kids, running again or getting through a workday. From there, your practitioner may use simple repeatable tests like strength, range of movement or balance, and short questionnaires about how pain affects your daily life.

These measures can show progress even when pain goes up and down. If things stall, we review the plan together, which might mean changing exercises, adding another service or referring you to your GP.

At Hybrid Physiotherapy, you'll know where you stand. Book online via the link in bio.

topic: New to Hybrid Physiotherapy? What to expect from your team

slides.headline: New here? Meet the team behind you
slides.sub: Physio, chiro, clinical Pilates and remedial massage under one roof.

slides.title: Physiotherapists
slides.body: Our physios assess how you move, explain what's likely going on and build an exercise-based plan. Hands-on treatment is used where it helps, alongside the exercises you do between visits.

slides.title: Chiropractors
slides.body: Our chiropractors assess your spine and joints and use hands-on care, including adjustments where appropriate, as one tool alongside exercise and practical advice for everyday life.

slides.title: Clinical Pilates team
slides.body: Our Pilates team runs supervised programs on the reformer and mat, tailored to your body and goals. It's a common next step as you build strength after an injury.

slides.title: Remedial massage therapists
slides.body: Our remedial massage therapists work on muscle tension and tightness. Massage can complement your active rehab and help you feel more comfortable as you get moving.

slides.title: We refer between each other
slides.body: If another service suits your problem better, or would help alongside your current care, we'll suggest it. You'll get a joined-up plan instead of starting from scratch.

slides.headline: Ready for your first visit?
slides.body: Choose the service that fits, or ask our admin team where to start. Chatswood and Sydney CBD.

caption:
